Shares of Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) fell more than 3 per cent in early trade on Friday as investors reacted to a fresh governance dispute at Tata Sons involving the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran and the proposed listing of the Tata Group’s holding company.

TCS shares declined as much as 3.64 per cent to Rs 2,116 on the BSE. Other Tata Group companies also came under pressure in early trade, with investors assessing the implications of the disagreement between Tata Trusts and the Tata Sons board.

The latest development follows Tata Sons’ September 17 board meeting, at which directors approved Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as executive chairman for another five-year term after the completion of his current tenure. The decision was passed by a majority, with Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata opposing the resolution.

Tata Trusts subsequently challenged the validity of the decision, maintaining that the reappointment was not in accordance with the holding company’s Articles of Association. The Trusts said their nominee directors must approve the appointment of the Tata Sons chairman and described the resolution as illegal.
The dispute extends beyond Chandrasekaran’s tenure to the future ownership structure of Tata Sons.

The Tata Sons board has moved to initiate steps towards complying with the Reserve Bank of India’s regulatory requirements relating to the listing of the holding company. The move follows the central bank’s rejection of Tata Sons’ request to retain its status as a private, unlisted company.
Tata Trusts, however, said it had not agreed to the proposed listing and argued that all available options should be examined before proceeding with a public issue.

In its statement, the Trusts reiterated its position that Tata Sons is fundamentally different from a conventional holding company because charitable trusts collectively hold around 66 per cent of its equity. It said dividends from Tata Group operating companies ultimately support philanthropic activities.
Noel Tata has also maintained that the group’s century-old structure, in which commercial operations and philanthropy are closely linked, should be preserved.
